# Credit the Gap Between Expected and Observed Yards to the Passer, and Read Agreement With Care

**What it is** — Burke's second variant estimates expected yards two ways: for the play configuration as a whole, or assuming each receiver is the target. Comparing what happened with the estimate, "we can credit that amount above or below expected to the quarterback's performance" (EeBgUCYhezc [12:23]). Example: Jared Goff (caption spelling "Jared Goff") was expected at 7.8 yards per attempt in 2018, actually had 9.9 on targeted passes, a difference of +2.1, credited to him (EeBgUCYhezc [12:54]). The 2018 top five and bottom five passers on this measure are shown on his chart (EeBgUCYhezc [12:54]).

He plots that residual against how often the passer agreed with the model's recommended target. Rookies sit low on production against expectation and high on agreement, which he reads as "the safe thing" and as the binding constraint on their offense (EeBgUCYhezc [13:33], [14:05]). The most aggressive passers sit on the left (EeBgUCYhezc [14:05]). He expected a positive correlation between agreement and production and found "slightly negative", which he explains as "a severe selection bias" (EeBgUCYhezc [14:38]). His reasoning: you cannot ask any quarterback to do what Aaron Rodgers would do, because he "may not have the physical attributes". The talk does not test this explanation.

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that the model holds the situation fixed, so whatever differs from expected belongs to the passer. He also says the credit is isolated "to a very large extent" from teammates but not from receivers or scheme (EeBgUCYhezc [20:52]). Inference: this is a residual method, and the residual absorbs everything the model leaves out (hands, height, vertical position, scheme, as he lists them at [22:01]).

**When to apply** — As a template for "expected versus observed" where a model can state what a typical athlete would produce in this situation. Inference: the same shape fits GPS (expected drill load versus observed). Always report what the residual cannot isolate.

Eric's baseline: "I think it's raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q12, about ACWR.) Inference: that skepticism toward a single ratio read without context applies equally to a residual credited to one person.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not read agreement with the model as decision quality: the talk's own data show it did not track production, and the explanation is unverified. The talk is single-season (2018 through week 12) NFL data and a "proof of concept" (EeBgUCYhezc [23:32]). Do not use a residual to rank individuals when the model lacks inputs that differ by individual. Marked untested because the speaker shows no validation of the credit, only the chart and one worked example.

**Contested** — [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]] (SSAC25, Ben Jenkins) argues that residuals from a prediction model rely on correlation and are not a causal estimate of player impact, which is the approach used here. The two talks use the data differently; this entry's method is a residual in exactly the sense that talk criticizes.

**Example** — Goff: 7.8 expected, 9.9 observed, +2.1 (EeBgUCYhezc [12:54]).

**Related** — [[claim--deepqb-target-accuracy-60-percent-against-20-percent-chance]]; [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]].

# A Quarterback-Specific Model by Transfer Learning: Reported Failure

**What it is** — Burke's fourth variant tries to capture one passer's tendencies. The motive he gives: "we don't have enough data for individual quarterbacks, they just don't have enough pass attempts" (EeBgUCYhezc [18:20]). The method (EeBgUCYhezc [18:50]):

1. Train all layers on the full data set, all quarterbacks.
2. Freeze the base layers.
3. Retrain on one quarterback only.

He compares the shared layers to a common intuitive sense of physics (everyone can drive without crashing) and the retrained layers to individual executive decision-making (EeBgUCYhezc [19:21]). The result: "not as well as I'd hoped". Drew Brees (as named) was the most similar quarterback to Drew Brees, but some of the best-performing quarterbacks were the least similar and some of the poorest performers the most similar, on target-decision similarity (EeBgUCYhezc [19:51]). He offers an explanation that Brees threw to running backs by design, while others do so "as a last resort" (EeBgUCYhezc [20:22]; the caption text here is garbled, so the explanation is uncertain). He reports it despite the result, calling this variant "pretty experimental" (EeBgUCYhezc [18:20]).

**Why it works** — It did not work as hoped, so there is no mechanism to give for success. The speaker gives the brain analogy above only as intent. Inference: with a few hundred passes per passer, even a frozen base leaves too little to fit person-specific layers.

**When to apply** — As a cautionary case when someone proposes a per-athlete model from a small pooled data set (a single Baylor quarterback, one athlete's force-plate history). Ask first what the athlete-level sample size is and how similarity will be checked.

Eric's baseline: Inference (no stated baseline line applies): Eric's baseline for individual thresholds is percent change from baseline or a rolling average with standard deviations and smallest worthwhile change (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q2a), which is a simple within-person method and not a pooled-model fine-tune.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one reported attempt, in one data set (2016 to 2018 NFL passes), with no reported metric beyond the similarity ranking, so it should not be cited as proof that transfer learning cannot work for individualized models. It is also not a recommendation to use it. The speaker's explanation for the odd similarity ordering is unverified.

**Example** — The talk's own: the top five and bottom five "similar quarterbacks" ranking, in which Brees is most similar to himself (EeBgUCYhezc [19:51]).

**Related** — [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]] (variant 4 is this); [[claim--deepqb-target-accuracy-60-percent-against-20-percent-chance]].

**What it is** — S Min Hong (caption spelling "s Min Hong", "S Hong"; an applied scientist at AWS) presents work with the NFL Next Gen Stats team that replaces end-of-play pass-rush counts with a pressure measure through the whole play (1nt8hK2oYrE [00:00], [01:02]). # Credit Pass-Rush Pressure Across the Whole Play, Not Only the Final Event

**What it is** — Hong's starting point: pass-rush statistics record only the outcome (sack, and counts of hits and hurries), so a rusher who closes on the quarterback but does not finish gets no credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [01:02], [01:34], [02:05]). The aim is to measure pressure "continuously applied throughout a play" and give credit to the defensive players who apply it (1nt8hK2oYrE [01:02], [02:38]). Outputs the speaker names: how long the passer is under pressure, and a "pressure zone", time with the score above 75 percent (1nt8hK2oYrE [14:34]).

In the example plays, three players generate high pressure, two early and one later who gets the sack (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00]), and in another the model credits two players with forcing the passer out of the pocket where "a human label" credited one (1nt8hK2oYrE [14:04]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no evidence the continuous credit is more accurate than the human label, only that it differs on his examples. Inference: counting outcomes only discards the time and path information that tracking data hold.

**When to apply** — When a coach's question is about a process that unfolds over a play and the available statistic records one endpoint. Ask whether tracking or film data can record the path, and who would act on it.

Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Eric-authored SportSmith, in method-baseline.md.) Inference: finer-grained credit is worth collecting only if it changes a decision about a player, and the talk reports no decision outcome.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: the evidence is two sample plays and no accuracy for the score itself (see [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]). It is NFL data and ignores scheme, double teams and stunts as credit modifiers (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). The speaker's own Q&A answers confirm the score does not say whose pressure it is (1nt8hK2oYrE [21:40]), so using it to rank individual rushers goes beyond what the talk shows. One panel questioner argued the metric should weight how early pressure arrives (a hurry at 3 seconds beats one at 5.5), and the speaker agreed it was a good point (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38], [20:09]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a play where two rushers create high pressure early and a third late "who eventually get the sack" (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00]).

**Related** — [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]]; [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]. Contrast with [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]] (SSAC25), which argues about what a credited number can mean and applies to this kind of per-player credit.

# Pressure Score: A Blocker-Interference Feature and a Forgiving Label

**What it is** — Stage 3 of Hong's pipeline (see [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]]) models pressure as a probability that a rusher gets a hit, hurry or sack, on a 0 to 1 scale "at any point in time during the play" (1nt8hK2oYrE [08:47], [09:19]). Two design choices are the useful part.

**1. A blocker-interference feature.** For each rusher, an "area of interest" is set by distance and angle between the rusher and the passer, and the number of blockers inside it is counted, to measure the resistance the rusher may meet (1nt8hK2oYrE [09:51], [10:23]). It sits alongside the static and dynamic tracking features from the matchup stage and relative position, velocity and acceleration to the passer (1nt8hK2oYrE [09:51], [23:43]).

**2. A forgiving target.** Targets are the manually labeled PFF hurry, hit and sack, plus an engineered label based on the rusher's distance to the passer at a point in time (1nt8hK2oYrE [10:23], [10:54]). In Q&A he describes it as one rusher getting within one yard of the passer before one second; the captions are garbled, so the exact rule is uncertain (1nt8hK2oYrE [20:39]). The reason he gives: "it is not always the one player gets a sack", so a rusher who gets into the threshold area earns credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [22:12]).

Main drivers he gives (a light feature analysis, no values stated): the rusher's relative position to the passer, velocity and acceleration, initial position (who starts close), and how many blockers the rusher faces, with an open rusher more likely to generate pressure (1nt8hK2oYrE [17:37], [18:08], [18:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the intent (credit more than the sack-taker) but no test of the engineered label. Inference: a distance-based label turns a rare event (sack) into a more frequent one, which gives a model more signal to learn from.

**When to apply** — When an event label is rare and a process variable (distance, time) is available: consider a second, softer label, and disclose how it was set. Count obstructions between a mover and a target as a feature when tracking is available.

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Eric-authored, Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: label consistency is the weakest point here; PFF hurry and hit labels are subjective hand labels, and the engineered label rule is not fully stated in the talk.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no accuracy figure, no feature weights, no validation of the engineered label. The model "didn't actively account for" complex position features (1nt8hK2oYrE [18:38]), and team scheme and strategies are left as future work (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). It was trained on NFL data and PFF labels. The speaker did not check correlation with quarterback motion (1nt8hK2oYrE [23:13]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a passer forced out of the pocket after heavy pressure, where the model credits two rushers (1nt8hK2oYrE [14:04]).

**Related** — [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]; [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]]; [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]].

# When the Output Is a Probability, Pick the Better-Calibrated Model

**What it is** — For the pressure score, Hong chose a random forest over "a complex neural network based or Transformer based model", because "model calibration" matters for a continuous score and the forest had better expected calibration error and maximum calibration error (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:26], [11:58], [12:28]). No calibration values are given.

He also notes an evaluation difficulty: a continuous pressure score is "kind of hard to evaluate", so he used a proxy, the maximum pressure a rusher or team puts on a passer, compared against PFF hurry, hit and sack labels, and reports "great accuracy" and better accuracy against hits and sacks, with a disparity across player groups and room to improve (the captions are garbled here; 1nt8hK2oYrE [10:54], [11:26], [11:58]).

**Why it works** — The speaker states calibration as the reason and gives no mechanism for why forests calibrate better than deep models here. Inference: a score read as a probability by a coach (for example, "70 percent chance this rusher gets home") is only honest if stated probabilities match observed frequencies.

**When to apply** — When model output will be shown as a probability or compared with a threshold (the talk uses a 75 percent "pressure zone" at 1nt8hK2oYrE [14:34]): compare candidate models on calibration error as well as accuracy, and prefer the simpler one when it calibrates better.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: a simple, inspectable model that Applied Performance staff can explain to coaches fits that rule better than a model nobody can interrogate.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no error values, no comparison table shown, only the speaker's statement. It applies to a probability output, and does not mean forests beat neural networks in general. The DeepQB talk (EeBgUCYhezc) used a feed-forward network and reported a calibration chart "fairly well calibrated" ([[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]]), so calibration is achievable with a neural network; the two talks do not compare.

**Example** — The speaker's choice itself: random forest over neural or Transformer models for the pressure score (1nt8hK2oYrE [12:28]).

**Related** — [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]; [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]; [[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]]; the CLIP talk also checks calibration and AUC for its propensity model, see [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]].

# Player Credit Is a Causal Question, Not a Prediction Residual

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins (senior data scientist at Sumer Sports, PhD student at Florida Atlantic University, pcp9h_M6Ir8 [00:00]) argues that "estimating player performance is fundamentally a causal problem yet it's often treated as a prediction problem" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [00:30]). The usual approach trains a model to predict an expected outcome (a conditional mean) and attributes the residual, actual minus predicted, to the player. His example is rush yards over expected: a back "expected to gain four yards" runs 26, and the 22-yard residual is credited to him (caption name "Damen Harris", pcp9h_M6Ir8 [02:00], [02:31]). Such metrics "solely rely on correlation based techniques" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:00]). He contrasts the two: machine learning predicts what is likely and "excels at pattern recognition", while causal inference "seeks to answer why and how something happens" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [02:31]). He claims, "based on our knowledge", this is the first public application of causal inference to the offensive line and one of few on NFL tracking data (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [00:00]).

**Why it works** — His stated reason is that a residual cannot say what would have happened under a different action by the player; the causal framing asks for the effect of the action on the outcome (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:00], [02:31]). The way he does it is in [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]].

**When to apply** — When a metric credits one player for an outcome that several teammates and opponents shaped (blocking, pressure, assist chains). Ask what the number conditions on, and whether it is a residual from a prediction model. Inference: this is a question to ask of vendor grades, and it applies to a residual such as the one in [[heuristic--credit-yards-above-expected-to-the-passer-with-selection-bias-caveat]].

Eric's baseline: "I think it's raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q12, about ACWR.) Inference: the same habit of asking what a single number leaves out is what this talk argues for; Eric's baseline has no causal-inference method of its own.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested. The talk is a method presentation by its builder (Sumer Sports), and its causal reading depends on assumptions the talk checks only partly (see [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]]). The DeepQB talk (EeBgUCYhezc [12:23]) and the many residual metrics the speaker names treat the residual as credit; this talk disagrees with that approach, and the library does not hold evidence that settles it. Inference: residual metrics and causal estimates answer different questions (how a player compares with typical, versus what his action did), and both can be useful for a screening or scouting decision, so the principle should not be read as "residuals are wrong". The talk also says residual metrics "are useful" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [09:05]). Validation shown is against honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not themselves a test of cause (see [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]).

**Example** — The speaker's: rush yards over expected on the handoff play, 4 expected and 26 gained, 22 attributed (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [02:00]).

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[heuristic--credit-yards-above-expected-to-the-passer-with-selection-bias-caveat]] (a residual method, contested by this principle); [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]] (per-player credit by a descriptive model). Vault paper on a related rating approach: [[pipping-gamon-2026-opponent-adjusted-evaluation-of-nfl-pass-blocking-and-pass-rushing-performance]].

# CLIP: A Doubly Robust Estimate of What Allowing Pressure Does to Completion

**What it is** — CLIP (caption versions: "causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays" and "...lineman..."; pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:30]) estimates how pressure allowed by an offensive lineman changes completion probability, per lineman, per play, every tenth of a second (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:30], [04:31]). Two models (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:01], [10:35]):

1. **Outcome model:** probability of a completed pass from features X and whether pressure was allowed.
2. **Propensity score model:** probability that the lineman allows pressure, from features X. Inverse propensity weighting uses it to build a more balanced data set for comparing outcomes (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [10:35]).

The estimator is called doubly robust because "it only requires one of the two models to be correctly specified" to identify the causal effect (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:01]). The captions name it "a w robust estimator" (garbled; the name is not confirmed here). The target is the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) per player per play: expected completion given pressure occurred minus expected completion given it did not, given features X (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:31]). Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a 0 to 1 probability, which is what lets his plots show shading (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [13:35]). Inputs are Big Data Bowl tracking data for all linemen, teammates and opponents, with the model "figure out what was important"; he accounts for proximity to the quarterback, to the nearest defenders and to nearby teammates, and for defenders' position, speed and distance to the quarterback (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [11:05], [11:35]). A questioner said the features were confusing (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [11:05]). Summarizing for a questioner: it analyzes the propensity to allow pressure combined with the impact on completion given pressure, "in simple terms" yes (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [10:05]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's two stated advantages: it is "robust to model misspecification" and it "helps reduce bias from confounding variables" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:31]). The talk gives no further mechanism for how the player-level credit is derived from the two models.

**When to apply** — As the reference when asking how a causal player metric is built from observational tracking data: name the treatment (pressure allowed), the outcome (completion), the two models, and the estimand (CATE). Its checks are in [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]].

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: the staff question that would justify this build is who on the offensive line is costing the offense, and the talk does not compare its cost with simpler views.

**When NOT to apply** — Needs play-level x,y tracking for all players at consistent quality, which the speaker says exists at the college level via computer vision (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [12:35]) but which the baseline's stack does not list. The public sample is the first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season (caption "2020 2021") from the 2023 Big Data Bowl (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:03]); no play counts, player counts or intervals are given. The speaker's feature handling is loose by his own account. Causal claims hold only if the model adjusts for what drives both pressure and completion, and this is checked partly (see the robustness entry). He works at Sumer Sports, so this is the builder's view.

**Example** — The two worked plays in [[case-study--clip-failed-block-versus-clean-protection-plays]].

**Related** — [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]]; [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]. Different tracking-data methods in this batch: [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]] (predicts who the quarterback throws to; a prediction model) and [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]] (scores a rusher's pressure; descriptive, no causal claim).

# Robustness Checks for a Causal Estimate: Balance, Placebo, Subsets, Sensitivity, Calibration

**What it is** — Jenkins says that with causal inference "you need to be able to run tests" to see how sensitive the result is to the assumptions (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]). The checks he reports for CLIP (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05], [08:35]):

1. **Covariate balance:** standardized mean differences "less than 0.1 after weighting", which he calls ideal.
2. **Placebo test:** replace the treatment with a placebo variable; the effect went to zero, which he says confirms the effect "is not due to chance".
3. **Random-subset consistency:** CATE values stayed consistent across random subsets of the data.
4. **Sensitivity analysis:** add unobserved confounding variables in simulation; CATE values varied by "less than a 3% variation".
5. **Calibration and AUC curves** for the propensity model, since it is used to predict probabilities.

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that if the causal effect is real, the estimate should remain stable across subsets and vanish when the treatment is swapped for a placebo (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]). He gives no mechanism for the sensitivity threshold. Inference: covariate balance after weighting is the direct check that the propensity model did its job of making treated and untreated plays comparable on the measured features.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a causal or "adjusted" player metric from observational data: ask for balance after weighting, a placebo or negative-control test, stability across subsets, and a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounders. Inference: the same checklist applies to any claim that a training exposure caused a monitoring change.

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Eric-authored, Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: robustness checks are the model-side version of that standard.

**When NOT to apply** — The reported figures are the speaker's, from a talk with no table, no play or player counts, no confidence intervals, and no definition of how the 3 percent variation was measured (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:35]). The simulated confounders are ones he chose, so passing the sensitivity check is not proof that no real unmeasured confounder (for example scheme, play design or quarterback skill, Inference) is missing. The checks do not show that the player-level credit is right, only that the aggregate estimate is stable.

**Example** — The placebo check: swapping in a placebo treatment sent the effect to zero (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]).

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]; calibration of a different model: [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]] and [[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]].

# CLIP Is Said to Beat Other Methods at Finding Top Linemen and Ranking by Salary

**What it is** — Jenkins reports three external comparisons (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [06:33], [07:03], [07:34]):

1. The causal model was "significantly better" at identifying top offensive linemen as indicated by All-Pro and Pro Bowl honors, shown as dark green shading in a chart.
2. It was "significantly better" in ranking players by salary, "much more consistent".
3. Aggregated on the 2023 Big Data Bowl sample, there is a "strong positive correlation" with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences he attributes to PFF having the entire data set while his team had the first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 season (caption "2020 2021").

He adds that the model correlates strongly with completion percentage on individual plays, so teams with better lines complete more passes and win more games over a season (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no numbers: "significantly" has no test statistic, no correlation coefficient and no sample size in the talk. Inference: agreement with honors, salary and PFF shows the metric resembles consensus judgment, which is not evidence that the credit is causal.

**When to apply** — As an example of what external validation a vendor presents. Ask for the correlation values, the sample, what happens when honors and salary are held out, and whether the model finds linemen the consensus misses (the question that matters for recruiting, Inference).

Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Eric-authored SportSmith, in method-baseline.md.) Inference: a method that mostly reproduces PFF rankings adds cost without new insight unless it disagrees with them usefully, and the talk does not show that.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no numbers back "significantly better", and honors and salary are shaped by the same reputation the model is compared with. The sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. The speaker is from the company that built the method. Do not use this entry to claim CLIP is more accurate than PFF grades.

**Example** — The comparison with PFF rankings on the 2023 Big Data Bowl sample, differing partly because PFF had the full season (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:03]).

**Related** — [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]]; [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]].

# Two CLIP Plays: A Failed Block and Clean Protection

**What it is** — Jenkins shows two plays, each with a field map shaded by each lineman's value, a time series every tenth of a second, and a whole-line value (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [04:31], [05:01]).

**Failed block.** A Tua Tagovailoa completion to a receiver (captions: "Tua tangaloa", "mik aeki") where two linemen "fail their assignment" and the quarterback is pressured. Green means above expectation and red below; the model flags the two linemen in red as lowering the chance of a successful play (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [04:01], [04:31]). Values change over time with each lineman's features. The whole-line value starts at 0.10 to 0.15 (captions "01 to 0.15"), read as 10 to 15 percent of the completion attributable to the line, something he says correlation-only metrics "cannot state" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [05:01]).

**Clean protection.** A Jimmy Garoppolo completion to Deebo Samuel (captions "Jimmy Garoppolo", "Debo Samuel") with plenty of space; shading runs purple to green because everyone contributed positively and no pressure was allowed. Best performers named: "Daniel brunskill" (caption spelling); one of the worst, Trent Williams, "but he's still positive". The line total is 0.6 to 0.8 (captions "6 to8"), read as 60 to 80 percent of the play attributable to the line (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [05:31], [06:01]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for why the line share differs so much between plays (10 to 15 percent versus 60 to 80 percent), and the talk does not explain it. Inference: because the estimand is the effect of allowing pressure, a play with no pressure allowed makes the positive values hard to interpret as that effect, and the speaker does not say how.

**When to apply** — As a worked pair to test understanding of the output: one can read a lineman's value as a play-level, time-varying credit. Inference: a usable film-review exercise is to check the two flagged linemen against film for the assignment failure the speaker describes.

Eric's baseline: Eric's baseline has no football-play method; the closest standing rule is "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.)

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: two hand-picked plays, one outcome each, no distribution of values, and no check that the model's read of "who failed" matches film beyond the speaker's statement that it "correctly" identified them (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [04:31]). The 10 to 15 versus 60 to 80 percent line shares are unexplained and the captions for both ranges are garbled, so the exact figures may differ. A single play is not evidence of accuracy.

**Example** — This entry is the example; see the two plays above.

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]; [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]]. Contrast with the pass-rush side example in [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]] (SSAC24).

# Moving an NFL Tracking Model to College: Adjust for Quality of Competition

**What it is** — A questioner asked whether the approach carries over to college, "especially" the G4 and G5 schools (Group of Four, Group of Five; caption spellings) versus NFL results (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [12:05], [12:35]). Jenkins answers that it could apply to college and Power-4 data, because computer vision gives actual tracking data at the college level, and that "an important consideration" is to account more for competition differences, since "quality of competition is going to be important in college more than NFL" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [12:35]). He suggests it as extendable to other positions and sports (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [09:35]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is only that opponents differ more in quality in college. He shows no adjustment and no college results. Inference: if linemen face very different opponents, an unadjusted credit mixes player skill with opponent strength.

**When to apply** — Before using any NFL-built model on Baylor or opponent data: ask the vendor how it adjusts for competition level, and whether the model was fit on college data. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance decisions and does not own the call (Eric-authored Playbook p.6, in method-baseline.md), so the practical step is to put this question to the vendor or the football staff's analyst before a number is shown to coaches.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: the answer is a statement, with no college application in the talk. The speaker did not say what the adjustment would be or whether tracking quality at the college level matches the NFL's. The method is the speaker's own and he works at Sumer Sports. The question and answer concern pass blocking only, and he did not discuss Baylor, a Big 12 program, or any specific conference.

**Example** — The Q&A exchange itself (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [12:05], [12:35]).

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]. DeepQB's limit of NFL-only data is in [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]].

I wrote 16 entries for the three talks into `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\staging\library\sports-analytics-and-decision-making\ssac-talks--42analytics\_batch_e\`. I did not run the review gate. I did spot-check for em dashes and for invented examples, and fixed the few I found. Each entry has the prompt's front matter and the six body sections, and every number carries a `<video-id> [mm:ss]` locator.

I wrote no `_book.md` or `_domain.md` files. The `_domain.md` already existed in the parent folder, and I left the book index to whoever merges the batches.

**Entries by kind and confidence**

| Talk | Entries | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| DeepQB (EeBgUCYhezc) | 2 frameworks (model inputs and variants; calibration and outcome checks), 1 claim (60% vs 20% chance, 74% vs 55% completion), 1 heuristic (yards-above-expected credit), 1 case-study (quarterback-specific transfer learning, a reported failure) | 3 supported, 1 untested, 1 contested |
| Pass rush (1nt8hK2oYrE) | 2 frameworks (three-stage pipeline; features and labels), 1 principle, 1 heuristic (calibrated random forest), 1 claim (evaluation and attribution limits) | 1 supported, 4 untested |
| Linemen (pcp9h_M6Ir8) | 3 frameworks, 1 principle, 1 claim, 1 case-study, 1 heuristic | 2 supported, 3 untested, 1 contested |

Totals: 7 frameworks, 2 principles, 3 claims, 2 heuristics... plus the others as listed above, which sum to 16 entries.

The three methods stay distinct: DeepQB predicts which receiver is targeted, the pass-rush work is a descriptive pressure score, and CLIP is a causal estimate for linemen. Each entry cross-links to the others in Related.

The causal-credit principle is `contested` against the DeepQB residual heuristic. The CLIP talk argues residual metrics rely on correlation, and DeepQB's method is exactly such a residual.

**Reciprocal-link suggestions**
- Vault paper `pipping-gamon-2026-opponent-adjusted-evaluation-of-nfl-pass-blocking-and-pass-rushing-performance` should link to the pass-rush pipeline framework and the causal-credit principle. My entries already link to it.
- Other batches' entries on quarterback or defensive tracking models, ACWR skepticism, or "data cost versus insight" should link back to the DeepQB and CLIP entries.
- The other `ssac-talks--42analytics` batches could link to the three calibration entries: the DeepQB checks, the random-forest heuristic, and the CLIP robustness checks.

**Unclear or contradictory spots in the transcripts**
- Pass rush: the demo plays credit individual players, but the Q&A says the model does not separate whose pressure it is [21:40]. I recorded both without picking one.
- Pass rush: the model type is garbled in the captions ("Orum", "autog glom"). The F1 values (0.99, 0.91) and the engineered "within one yard before one second" label rule are caption-rough.
- CLIP: the line shares of 0.10 to 0.15 versus 0.6 to 0.8 are caption-garbled and the talk never explains the gap. The estimator name ("a w robust estimator") is garbled.
- DeepQB: the explanation for the odd similarity ranking (Brees throwing to running backs) is garbled at [20:22]. The Q&A answer about reviewing results with quarterbacks is also garbled.
- Names and numbers are kept as caption spellings and flagged as such.

I could read everything I needed. I used `method-baseline.md` only for the "Eric's baseline:" lines and kept its Explicit and interview tags.
